t: ω (omega)
d: A frequency — how fast something wiggles, in radians per second. · said OH-may-ga

t: ω₀ (omega-nought)
d: The natural frequency: the rhythm a system wants to oscillate at if nothing damped it. · said OH-may-ga zero

t: ω_d (omega-d)
d: The frequency you actually see wobbling, once damping has slowed it down a bit. · said OH-may-ga dee

t: δ (delta)
d: In your lecture slides and in the question text of your papers, the damping factor. This course writes that quantity as ζ. · said DEL-ta

t: η (eta)
d: The viscous friction coefficient: how much force a damper pushes back with, per unit of speed. · said AY-ta

t: ζ (zeta)
d: The damping factor, also called the damping ratio: how strongly friction kills the oscillation. A pure number with no units. · said ZAY-ta

t: τ (tau)
d: The time constant: how long a first-order system takes to get 63 % of the way to its final value. · said rhymes with "now" or "saw"

t: Δ (capital delta)
d: Means "a small change in". Δh means "a small change in the height h". · said DEL-ta

t: µ (mu)
d: The integrating factor: the thing you multiply a differential equation by so that two terms fuse into one derivative. · said MEW

t: σ (sigma, lowercase)
d: Usually the real part of a pole — how fast something decays. Also, with a (t) after it, the unit step. · said SIG-ma

t: Σ (sigma, capital)
d: Means "add all of these up". · said SIG-ma

t: φ (phi)
d: An angle, usually a phase angle in degrees. · said FYE or FEE

t: π (pi)
d: The circle number, 3.14159... · said PIE

t: ρ (rho)
d: Density — how much mass fits into a given volume. · said ROH

t: ∞ (infinity)
d: Endlessly large, or "after waiting forever". · said in-FIN-it-ee

t: ε (epsilon)
d: A tiny amount — "as small as you like, but not quite zero". · said EP-sil-on

t: ∠ (angle)
d: The phase of a complex number or a transfer function: the angle its arrow makes, measured from the positive real axis. · said the angle of

t: √ (square root)
d: The number which, multiplied by itself, gives what is under the bar. · said square root

t: ± (plus-minus)
d: Both answers at once: do it with + and again with −. · said plus or minus

t: × (times)
d: Multiply. · said times

t: ÷ (divide)
d: Divide. · said divided by

t: ≡ (identically)
d: Stronger than equals: true for every value, not solved at one. · said identically

t: ° (degrees)
d: The unit an angle is quoted in when it is not in radians. · said degrees

t: · (centre dot)
d: Also means multiply. · said times

t: ≈ (approximately)
d: Nearly equal — close enough for our purposes. · said approximately equals

t: → (arrow)
d: Leads to, or tends towards. · said goes to / gives

t: ⇒ (double arrow)
d: Because of the line before, the line after must be true. · said therefore / implies

t: ⟺ (if and only if)
d: Both directions are true: each one guarantees the other. · said if and only if

t: ≤ ≥ (less/greater or equal)
d: Smaller than (or the same as), or bigger than (or the same as). · said less than or equal to

t: ≠ (not equal)
d: These two things are different. · said not equal to

t: ⁄ (crossed out)
d: This term has been cancelled and is gone from the next line. · said cancelled

t: ẋ (a dot on top)
d: The rate of change of x — how fast x is changing right now. · said "x dot"

t: d/dt
d: The same thing as a dot: "how fast is this changing". · said "dee by dee tee"

t: derivative
d: A rate of change. The slope of a graph at one point.

t: ∂ (partial derivative)
d: A derivative when there is more than one variable, and you change only ONE of them. · said "partial dee" or "curly dee"

t: ∫ (integral)
d: The running total. The opposite of a derivative. · said IN-teg-ral

t: lim
d: The value something creeps towards. · said "limit"

t: δ(t) (Dirac impulse)
d: An input signal: one instantaneous kick, of zero width and area 1. The only δ in this course — the damping factor is ζ. · said di-RAK DEL-ta
s: the impulse - NOT the damping factor

t: 1(t) (unit step)
d: An input signal: zero before t = 0, one afterwards, for ever. Flipping a switch. · said the unit step

t: s
d: The Laplace variable. Think of it as a stand-in for "d/dt". · said ess

t: Laplace transform
d: A trick that turns calculus into algebra. · said la-PLAHSS

t: transfer function G(s)
d: Output divided by input, in the s-world. It fully describes how a system responds.

t: pole
d: A value of s that makes the bottom of G(s) equal zero.

t: zero
d: A value of s that makes the TOP of G(s) equal zero.

t: numerator
d: The top part of a fraction. · said NEW-mer-ay-tor

t: denominator
d: The bottom part of a fraction. · said de-NOM-in-ay-tor

t: characteristic equation
d: The denominator of the closed loop, set equal to zero.

t: DC gain, G(0)
d: What the output settles at for an input of 1. Just put s = 0 into G(s).

t: strictly proper
d: The bottom of the fraction has a higher power of s than the top.

t: PT1
d: A first-order lag. One energy store. Smooth rise, never overshoots. · said pee-tee-one

t: PT2
d: A second-order system. Two energy stores. CAN overshoot and wobble. · said pee-tee-two

t: IT1
d: An integrator with a lag in front of it. Output ramps up forever. · said eye-tee-one

t: dead time Tₜ
d: A pure delay. Nothing happens at all for a while, then the response starts.

t: order
d: The highest power of s in the denominator. Also: how many energy stores the system has.

t: step response
d: What the output does when you suddenly switch the input from 0 to 1 and leave it there.

t: impulse response
d: What the output does after a single instantaneous kick.

t: overshoot M_p
d: How far past the target the output goes before coming back, usually as a percentage.

t: peak time T_m
d: How long until the output reaches its highest point.

t: return time T₅%
d: How long until the output stops straying more than 5 % from its final value.

t: steady-state error e∞
d: How far off the target you still are after everything has settled down.

t: asymptotically stable
d: Left alone, the system settles down to a steady value.

t: marginally stable
d: It neither settles nor blows up — it wobbles forever at constant size.

t: left half plane (LHP)
d: The left side of the pole graph, where the real part is negative.

t: right half plane (RHP)
d: The right side of the pole graph, where the real part is positive.

t: Routh criterion
d: A table that tells you if a system is stable WITHOUT finding the roots. · said ROWTH (rhymes with mouth)

t: Nyquist criterion
d: A stability test done by drawing G(jω) as a curve in the complex plane. · said NYE-kwist

t: phase / gain margin
d: How much room you have left before the loop becomes unstable.

t: open loop
d: No measurement, no feedback. The controller acts blind.

t: closed loop
d: The output is measured and fed back, so the controller reacts to what actually happened.

t: plant G_S
d: The physical thing you are trying to control and cannot change.

t: controller G_R
d: The only block in the loop you get to design. It reads the error and decides what to do about it.

t: setpoint W
d: The value you WANT the output to be.

t: controlled variable Y
d: The thing you actually care about and are measuring.

t: manipulated variable U
d: The knob the controller turns.

t: disturbance Z
d: Anything outside the loop that pushes the output around.

t: control error E
d: Setpoint minus measured value. How wrong you currently are.

t: K_R (controller gain)
d: How hard the controller pushes for a given error.

t: T_N (reset time)
d: Sets how strong the integral action is. SMALL T_N = STRONG I action.

t: T_V (rate time)
d: Sets how strong the derivative action is. BIG T_V = STRONG D action.

t: PID controller
d: Three actions added together: P reacts to now, I to the past, D predicts the future. · said pee-eye-dee

t: system type
d: How many integrators (poles at s = 0) are in the open loop.

t: linearisation
d: Replacing a curve with the straight line that touches it at one point.

t: operating point
d: The steady state you are working around: nothing is changing.

t: Taylor expansion
d: Approximating a curve near a point using its value plus its slope. · said TAY-lor

t: state variable
d: Whatever sits inside the derivative — the things the system "remembers".

t: balance equation
d: accumulation = what comes in − what goes out.

t: constitutive law
d: The physical rule for one component. Ohm's law, Hooke's law, Newton's law. · said con-STIT-you-tiv

t: Torricelli’s law
d: Water squirts out of a hole at speed √(2gh). · said torri-CHELL-ee

t: coefficient
d: The number multiplying a symbol. · said co-eh-FISH-ent

t: polynomial
d: A sum of powers, like s³ + 4s² + 21s + 34. · said polly-NOH-mee-al

t: α (alpha)
d: Not a named quantity in this course. It is a stand-in: a constant whose value is given by the line that introduces it. · said AL-fa

t: θ (theta)
d: An angle. Which angle depends on the picture, and every picture that uses it says. · said THAY-ta

t: ϑ (theta, curly)
d: A temperature measured as a rise above something else, rather than on an absolute scale. · said THAY-ta

t: Ω (ohm)
d: The unit of resistance. A capital omega, and nothing to do with the lowercase ω that means a frequency. · said OHM

t: ′ (prime)
d: A rate of change, written the other way. f′ means the same as the dot over a letter. · said prime

t: λ (lambda)
d: A characteristic root: a value that makes the homogeneous equation work with y = e^(λt). · said LAM-da

t: root
d: A value that makes an expression equal zero.

t: complex number
d: A number with two parts: a normal part and an "imaginary" part written with j.

t: j (the imaginary unit)
d: A made-up number defined so that j × j = −1. · said jay

t: |G| (magnitude)
d: The size of a complex number: how far it is from the origin. · said mod G

t: decibel (dB)
d: A way of writing gain on a squashed scale: 20·log₁₀(gain). · said DESS-i-bell

t: e (Euler’s number)
d: The number 2.71828..., the natural base for growth and decay. · said ee

t: matrix
d: A grid of numbers, used to write several equations at once. · said MAY-trix

t: eigenvalue
d: A special number belonging to a matrix. For us: the same thing as a pole. · said EYE-gen-value

t: determinant, det()
d: One number squeezed out of a square grid of numbers.
